statute_title: Operating Under the Influence of an Intoxicant or Other Drug (OWI)
offense_class: Civil Forfeiture (first); Misdemeanor (second/third); Class H Felony (fourth); Class G Felony (fifth/sixth); Class F Felony (seventh/eighth); Class E Felony (ninth/tenth); Class D Felony (eleventh+)
penalty_max: Civil forfeiture only (first); 6 months (second); 1 year (third); 6 years (fourth); 10 years (fifth/sixth); 12.5 years (seventh+)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle on a public highway
While under the influence of an intoxicant, controlled substance, or other drug
Or with a BAC of .08 or higher (prohibited alcohol concentration)
Or with a detectable amount of a restricted controlled substance in blood
enhancements: BAC .17 or higher (doubled minimum penalties on second offense)
Passenger under 16 (enhanced penalties — additional 6 months maximum, § 346.65(2)(f))
Prior OWI homicide or injury conviction (enhanced sentencing)
Causing great bodily harm (Class F Felony under § 940.25)
notes: Wisconsin is the only state where first-offense OWI is a civil forfeiture (non-criminal) unless a passenger under 16 is present. Implied consent under § 343.305. Administrative license revocation 6-9 months.

offense_class: Civil Forfeiture (not criminal)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle on a public highway
While under the influence of an intoxicant or drugs
BAC .08 or higher
No prior OWI convictions
mandatory_minimum: $150 forfeiture; 6-9 month license revocation; Alcohol assessment
enhancements: Passenger under 16 (criminal misdemeanor — up to 6 months jail)
notes: First-offense OWI in Wisconsin is NOT a criminal offense — it is a civil forfeiture. No jail time unless a child under 16 is in the vehicle. License revocation 6-9 months. Ignition interlock if BAC .15+.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (second/third); Felony (fourth+)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle on a public highway
While under the influence of an intoxicant or drugs
BAC .08 or higher
One or more prior OWI convictions (lifetime lookback)
enhancements: BAC .17+ on second offense (doubled mandatory minimum to 10 days)
notes: Wisconsin uses a lifetime lookback for OWI counts. Fourth offense is Class H Felony regardless of when priors occurred. Ignition interlock required 1-4 years. Mandatory AODA assessment.

statute_title: OWI — Drugs or Restricted Controlled Substance
offense_class: Same as alcohol OWI by offense count
penalty_max: Same as alcohol OWI by offense count
fine_max: Same as alcohol OWI by offense count
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle on a public highway
While under the influence of a controlled substance or other drug
Or with a detectable amount of a restricted controlled substance in blood (per se — § 346.63(1)(am))
Restricted substances include THC, cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, PCP
mandatory_minimum: Same as alcohol OWI by offense count
enhancements: Combined influence of alcohol and drugs
Detectable amount of restricted controlled substance (per se violation)
notes: Wisconsin has a per se drugged driving law — any detectable amount of certain restricted controlled substances (delta-9-THC, cocaine, heroin, meth, PCP) is a violation. No threshold needed.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Felony — Class I (if causing great bodily harm)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
In a manner that endangered the safety of any person or property
With a wanton disregard for safety
enhancements: Causing great bodily harm (Class I Felony)
notes: Common plea-down from OWI. Points added to driving record. May result in license suspension.

statute_title: Duty to Stop at Scene of Accident — Injury or Death
offense_class: Class H Felony (injury); Class D Felony (death)
elements: Defendant was the operator of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in injury or death of any person
Defendant knowingly failed to stop at the scene
Defendant failed to provide identification and render aid
notes: Hit-and-run involving death is a Class D Felony. Property damage only hit-and-run is a civil forfeiture. License revocation upon conviction.

statute_title: Homicide by Intoxicated Use of a Vehicle
offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while under the influence of an intoxicant or drugs
Or with a prohibited alcohol concentration
Defendant's operation of the vehicle caused the death of another person
notes: Mandatory minimum 5 years imprisonment. OWI homicide is one of the most serious OWI-related charges. License revocation 5 years.

statute_title: Homicide by Negligent Operation of a Vehicle
offense_class: Class G Felony
elements: Defendant operated a vehicle in a criminally negligent manner
Defendant's operation caused the death of another person
notes: Negligent homicide by vehicle does not require intoxication — criminal negligence is sufficient. Less serious than OWI homicide.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Misdemeanor (subsequent — enhanced)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
While defendant's operating privilege was suspended or revoked
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
notes: OWI-related license suspension driving carries enhanced penalties. Additional suspension period upon conviction.

statute_title: Attempting to Flee or Elude an Officer
offense_class: Class I Felony (basic); Class H Felony (if endangering safety); Class F Felony (if death results)
penalty_max: 3.5 years (Class I); 6 years (Class H); 12.5 years (Class F)
elements: A traffic officer signaled the defendant to stop
Defendant knowingly fled or attempted to elude the officer
By driving at high speed or operating in a reckless manner
enhancements: Endangering safety of others (Class H Felony)
notes: Fleeing is always a felony in Wisconsin. Class F Felony if fleeing results in death of another person.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (most first offenses); Class I Felony (certain substances or second+)
penalty_max: 1 year (misdemeanor); 3.5 years (Class I Felony for second+)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed a controlled substance
Without a valid prescription
Substance is listed in Schedules I through V
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class I Felony)
Possession near a school, park, or public housing (sentence doubles under § 961.495)
notes: First-offense simple possession of most controlled substances is a misdemeanor. Second or subsequent is a Class I Felony. Drug court and diversion programs available.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Class I Felony (second+)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed tetrahydrocannabinols (THC)
Any amount
Without lawful authority
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class I Felony)
notes: Wisconsin has not legalized recreational or medical marijuana at the state level. First offense THC possession is a misdemeanor with up to 6 months and $1,000 fine. Some municipalities have local ordinances with lesser penalties.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Class I Felony (second+)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed cocaine or cocaine base
Cocaine is a Schedule II controlled substance
Without a valid prescription
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class I Felony)
notes: Crack cocaine (cocaine base) is treated the same as powder cocaine under Wisconsin law for possession.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Class I Felony (second+)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed methamphetamine
Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance
Without a valid prescription
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class I Felony)
notes: Manufacturing methamphetamine is a separate Class F Felony under § 961.41(1)(e). Possession of precursors for meth production also criminalized.

offense_class: Class F Felony (1-5g); Class E Felony (5-15g); Class D Felony (15-40g); Class C Felony (40g+)
penalty_max: 12.5 years (Class F); 15 years (Class E); 25 years (Class D); 40 years (Class C)
elements: Defendant manufactured, distributed, or delivered
Cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, or other Schedule I/II narcotic
Amount determines felony class
enhancements: Within 1,000 feet of school, park, or public housing (sentence doubles)
notes: Wisconsin uses weight-based tiers for trafficking penalties. School zone enhancement doubles the sentence. Conspiracy to deliver carries same penalties.

statute_title: Manufacturing or Delivering a Controlled Substance — Non-Narcotic
offense_class: Class H Felony (most Schedule I-IV); Class I Felony (Schedule V)
elements: Defendant manufactured, distributed, or delivered
A non-narcotic controlled substance
From Schedule I through V
notes: THC (marijuana) delivery of 200g-1000g is a Class I Felony; over 10,000g is a Class F Felony. Non-narcotic schedule penalties vary by weight.

offense_class: Class F Felony
elements: Defendant manufactured or attempted to manufacture methamphetamine
Through chemical synthesis or extraction
enhancements: Child under 18 in area of manufacturing (additional enhancement)
Clandestine lab near school or residence
notes: Mandatory minimum 3 years. Cleanup costs assessed against defendant. Child endangerment charges added if minors present.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (use/possession); Class I Felony (delivery to minor)
elements: Defendant possessed drug paraphernalia
Knowing or intending it to be used for manufacturing, testing, or consuming a controlled substance
enhancements: Delivery of paraphernalia to a minor (Class I Felony under § 961.574)
notes: Paraphernalia possession is a misdemeanor with relatively low penalties. Delivery to a minor is a felony.

offense_class: Varies by substance and weight: Class F to Class I Felony
penalty_max: 12.5 years (Class F for narcotic); 6 years (Class H); 3.5 years (Class I)
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
With intent to manufacture or deliver
Intent may be inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, or other evidence
enhancements: Near school, park, or public housing (sentence doubles)
notes: Possession with intent is charged based on substance type and weight. Penalties mirror delivery statutes. Intent inferred from totality of circumstances.

offense_class: Class A Felony
penalty_max: Life imprisonment without the possibility of extended supervision (parole)
elements: Defendant caused the death of another human being
With intent to kill that person or another
mandatory_minimum: Life imprisonment (parole eligibility after 20 years unless court sets later date)
enhancements: Court may deny extended supervision eligibility (life without parole)
Victim is a law enforcement officer, firefighter, or judge
notes: Wisconsin's only Class A Felony. Mandatory life sentence. Court determines extended supervision eligibility date (minimum 20 years). Wisconsin does not have the death penalty.

offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another human being
Under circumstances showing utter disregard for human life
enhancements: Use of a dangerous weapon (additional 5 years under § 939.63)
notes: Wisconsin does not use 'second-degree murder.' First-degree reckless homicide is the equivalent. Requires 'utter disregard for human life' — higher than ordinary recklessness.

offense_class: Class B Felony (mitigated from Class A)
elements: Defendant caused the death of another human being
With intent to kill
Under the influence of adequate provocation
notes: Wisconsin does not have a separate voluntary manslaughter statute. Adequate provocation is a mitigating defense that reduces first-degree intentional homicide to a Class B Felony.

offense_class: Class D Felony
elements: Defendant recklessly caused the death of another human being
Ordinary recklessness (not utter disregard for human life)
notes: Wisconsin's equivalent of involuntary manslaughter. Requires criminal recklessness but not the 'utter disregard' needed for first-degree reckless homicide.

statute_title: Aggravated Battery — Causing Great Bodily Harm with Intent
offense_class: Class E Felony
elements: Defendant caused great bodily harm to another person
By an act done with intent to cause great bodily harm
enhancements: Use of a dangerous weapon (additional 5 years under § 939.63)
notes: Wisconsin's most serious battery charge. 'Great bodily harm' includes injuries creating substantial risk of death, serious permanent disfigurement, or permanent loss of function.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant caused bodily harm to another person
By an act done with intent to cause bodily harm
Without the consent of the victim
enhancements: Domestic abuse modifier (additional 2 years if felony)
notes: Simple battery is a Class A Misdemeanor — the most serious misdemeanor in Wisconsin. 'Bodily harm' means physical pain or injury, illness, or impairment of physical condition.

statute_title: Substantial Battery — Causing Substantial Bodily Harm
offense_class: Class I Felony
elements: Defendant caused substantial bodily harm to another person
By an act done with intent to cause bodily harm
notes: 'Substantial bodily harm' means bodily injury that causes a laceration requiring stitches, any fracture of a bone, a burn, temporary loss of a bodily function, or a concussion.

offense_class: Class E Felony
elements: Defendant took property from the person or presence of the owner
By use or threat of use of force against the person of the owner
With intent to steal
enhancements: Use of dangerous weapon (armed robbery — Class C Felony)
Use of force that may cause bodily harm
notes: Basic robbery in Wisconsin is a Class E Felony. Armed robbery is significantly enhanced.

offense_class: Class C Felony
elements: Defendant committed robbery
While armed with a dangerous weapon or any article used or fashioned as a weapon
enhancements: Use of a firearm (additional 5 years mandatory minimum under § 939.63)
notes: Armed robbery is one of the most seriously punished property crimes. Firearm enhancer adds mandatory minimum consecutive time.

offense_class: Class C Felony (basic); Class B Felony (with bodily harm or ransom)
elements: Defendant seized and carried away another person
By force or threat of imminent force
Without the person's consent
enhancements: Bodily harm to victim (Class B Felony)
notes: False imprisonment (§ 940.30) is a Class H Felony. Taking hostages (§ 940.305) is a Class C Felony.

offense_class: Class C Felony (building); Class F Felony (property other than building)
elements: Defendant intentionally damaged a building
By means of fire
Without the consent of all persons with an interest in the building
enhancements: Building occupied at the time of fire
notes: Arson of a building is a Class C Felony regardless of whether it is a dwelling. Arson of other property (§ 943.03) is Class F Felony.

offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant had intent to kill another person
Defendant performed acts demonstrating unequivocal intent to kill
The killing was not completed
enhancements: Use of a dangerous weapon (additional 5 years)
notes: Attempted murder in Wisconsin is a Class B Felony — the same class as first-degree reckless homicide. Maximum penalty is the maximum for the attempted offense.

statute_title: Reckless Use of a Weapon / Battery with Dangerous Weapon
offense_class: Class G Felony (reckless endangerment with weapon); Class H Felony (battery with weapon enhancer)
penalty_max: 10 years (Class G); 6 years + 5 year enhancer (Class H + weapon)
elements: Defendant recklessly endangered safety by use of a dangerous weapon
Or committed battery while armed with a dangerous weapon
enhancements: Dangerous weapon enhancer adds up to 5 additional years (§ 939.63)
notes: Wisconsin does not have a separate 'assault with a deadly weapon' statute. Such conduct is charged as battery with a dangerous weapon enhancer or reckless endangerment.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (under $2,500); Class I Felony ($2,500-$5,000); Class H Felony ($5,000-$10,000); Class G Felony ($10,000+)
penalty_max: 9 months (Class A Misdemeanor); 3.5 years (Class I); 6 years (Class H); 10 years (Class G)
elements: Defendant intentionally took and carried away movable property of another
Without the owner's consent
With intent to permanently deprive the owner
enhancements: From a person (Class G Felony regardless of value)
notes: Wisconsin uses a tiered theft system based on value. Theft from the person (pickpocketing) is always a Class G Felony.

offense_class: Class I Felony ($2,500-$5,000); Class H Felony ($5,000-$10,000); Class G Felony ($10,000-$100,000); Class F Felony ($100,000+)
penalty_max: 3.5 years (Class I); 6 years (Class H); 10 years (Class G); 12.5 years (Class F)
elements: Defendant committed theft of property or services
Value exceeds $2,500
notes: Wisconsin does not use the term 'grand theft.' Felony theft begins at $2,500. Values over $100,000 are Class F Felony.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant committed theft of property or services
Value does not exceed $2,500
notes: Misdemeanor theft threshold is $2,500. Restitution typically ordered.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (under $500); Class I Felony ($500-$5,000); Class H Felony ($5,000-$10,000); Class G Felony ($10,000+)
penalty_max: 9 months (Class A); 3.5 years (Class I); 6 years (Class H); 10 years (Class G)
elements: Defendant intentionally took and carried away, transferred, or concealed merchandise
From a retail establishment
Without payment and with intent to permanently deprive
enhancements: Use of device to defeat security
notes: Wisconsin has a separate retail theft statute with lower felony thresholds than general theft ($500 vs $2,500). Civil recovery available to retailers.

offense_class: Class F Felony
elements: Defendant intentionally entered a building
Without the consent of the person in lawful possession
With intent to commit a felony therein
enhancements: Armed with a dangerous weapon (Class E Felony under § 943.10(2)(a))
Battery to someone in the building (Class E Felony)
notes: Basic burglary in Wisconsin is a Class F Felony. Armed burglary or burglary with battery is elevated to Class E Felony.

offense_class: Class F Felony
elements: Defendant intentionally entered a dwelling
Without the consent of the person in lawful possession
With intent to commit a felony therein
enhancements: Armed with dangerous weapon (Class E Felony)
Person present in dwelling (enhanced sentencing consideration)
notes: Wisconsin does not separately classify residential burglary — the same statute covers all buildings. Sentencing may be enhanced if it is a dwelling.

offense_class: Class H Felony (driving); Class I Felony (riding); Class A Misdemeanor (if abandoned undamaged)
elements: Defendant intentionally took and drove a motor vehicle
Without the consent of the owner
notes: Wisconsin uses 'operating vehicle without owner's consent' rather than 'motor vehicle theft.' Includes joyriding. Class H Felony for the driver, Class I for passengers who know the vehicle is stolen.

offense_class: Same tiers as theft by value: Class A Misdemeanor (under $2,500) through Class F Felony ($100,000+)
elements: Defendant intentionally received, retained, or disposed of stolen property
Knowing the property was stolen
notes: Penalties mirror general theft statute value tiers. Knowledge that property was stolen must be proven.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (under $2,500); Class I Felony ($2,500+); Class H Felony (if reduces value by $2,500+)
elements: Defendant intentionally caused damage to physical property of another
Without the owner's consent
enhancements: Damage to religious or educational property (Class I Felony regardless of amount)
notes: Felony threshold is $2,500 in damages. Graffiti specifically addressed under § 943.017. Restitution required.

offense_class: Class B Forfeiture (civil); Class A Misdemeanor (if warning given)
penalty_max: $1,000 forfeiture; 9 months (misdemeanor for subsequent or after warning)
elements: Defendant entered or remained on land of another
After being notified not to enter or remain
Through verbal warning, posted signs, or fencing
enhancements: Trespass to a dwelling (Class A Misdemeanor under § 943.14)
notes: Trespass to land is initially a civil forfeiture. Trespass to a dwelling (§ 943.14) is always a Class A Misdemeanor.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (under $2,500); Class I Felony ($2,500+)
elements: Defendant intentionally caused damage to physical property of another
Without the owner's consent
notes: Wisconsin uses 'criminal damage to property' for what other states call 'criminal mischief.' Value of damage determines the penalty tier.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (simple battery); enhanced by domestic abuse surcharge and modifier
penalty_max: 9 months (simple battery); additional 2 years if felony with DV modifier (§ 939.621)
elements: Defendant caused bodily harm to a spouse, former spouse, person with child in common, or cohabitant
With intent to cause bodily harm
enhancements: Domestic abuse modifier adds up to 2 years on felony charges (§ 939.621)
notes: Wisconsin has a mandatory arrest policy for domestic abuse. 72-hour no-contact period. $100 domestic abuse surcharge. Strangulation is a standalone felony.

offense_class: Class I Felony + domestic abuse modifier (additional 2 years)
elements: Defendant caused substantial bodily harm to a family or household member
With intent to cause bodily harm
notes: Felony domestic battery in Wisconsin is charged as substantial or aggravated battery with the domestic abuse modifier. Federal firearms prohibition applies.

statute_title: Neglecting a Child — Contributing to Delinquency
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (basic); Class F Felony (if death results); Class H Felony (if bodily harm results)
penalty_max: 9 months (misdemeanor); 6 years (Class H if bodily harm); 12.5 years (Class F if death)
elements: Defendant was a person responsible for a child's welfare
Defendant failed to exercise ordinary care to prevent bodily harm or death
notes: Wisconsin also charges child endangerment under § 948.21 and recklessly endangering safety (§ 941.30) when a child is the victim.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (bodily harm); Class H Felony (great bodily harm — reckless); Class F Felony (great bodily harm — intentional)
penalty_max: 9 months (Class A); 6 years (Class H); 12.5 years (Class F)
elements: Defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to a child
Or recklessly caused great bodily harm to a child
Or intentionally caused great bodily harm to a child
notes: Intentional great bodily harm to a child is a Class F Felony. Chronic child abuse (repeated acts) is a standalone Class H Felony.

statute_title: Violation of a Domestic Abuse Restraining Order
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class I Felony (second+ within 72 months or assault during violation)
elements: A valid domestic abuse restraining order or injunction was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant knowingly violated the order
enhancements: Second or subsequent violation within 72 months (Class I Felony)
notes: Includes temporary restraining orders and final injunctions. Violation of a harassment injunction (§ 813.125) carries similar penalties.

offense_class: Class I Felony (basic); Class H Felony (second+ or with weapon); Class F Felony (causing bodily harm)
penalty_max: 3.5 years (Class I); 6 years (Class H); 12.5 years (Class F)
elements: Defendant intentionally engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific person
That would cause a reasonable person to suffer serious emotional distress or fear of bodily harm or death
Defendant knew or should have known the conduct would cause fear
enhancements: Use of dangerous weapon (Class H Felony)
notes: Stalking is always a felony in Wisconsin. Course of conduct means two or more acts carried out over time. Cyberstalking included.

offense_class: Class B Forfeiture (first); Class A Misdemeanor (after warning or injunction)
elements: Defendant, with intent to harass or intimidate another person
Engaged in a course of conduct that served no legitimate purpose
And would cause a reasonable person to feel harassed, threatened, or intimidated
enhancements: Violation of harassment injunction (Class A Misdemeanor)
Use of telephone or electronic communication for harassment (§ 947.0125)
notes: First-offense harassment is a civil forfeiture. Criminal penalties apply if the defendant violates a harassment injunction.

offense_class: Class I Felony (basic); Class H Felony (great bodily harm or repeated)
elements: Defendant was a caregiver for an elder or vulnerable adult
Defendant intentionally subjected the elder to cruel maltreatment
Or caused bodily harm or neglected the elder's basic needs
notes: Financial exploitation of an elder is charged under the general theft statute with 'vulnerable adult' status as an aggravator.

statute_title: Possession of a Firearm by a Prohibited Person
offense_class: Class G Felony
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
Defendant was prohibited from possessing firearms (convicted felon, adjudicated delinquent, subject to DV injunction, involuntary commitment)
enhancements: Possession during commission of a felony
notes: Mandatory minimum 3 years imprisonment for felon in possession. Prohibited persons include convicted felons, persons adjudicated delinquent for certain offenses, and persons subject to DV injunctions.

statute_title: Felon in Possession of a Firearm
offense_class: Class G Felony
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
Defendant had previously been convicted of a felony in Wisconsin or any other jurisdiction
enhancements: Possession during commission of another felony
notes: Mandatory minimum 3 years. Cannot be reduced by sentencing adjustment or early release. Federal felon-in-possession (18 U.S.C. § 922(g)) may also apply.

statute_title: Carrying a Concealed Weapon Without a License
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class G Felony (if prohibited person)
elements: Defendant carried a concealed and dangerous weapon
Without a valid concealed carry license
Not in defendant's own dwelling or place of business
notes: Wisconsin enacted concealed carry in 2011. CCW license required. Open carry is legal without a license for non-prohibited persons.

statute_title: Endangering Safety by Use of a Dangerous Weapon
offense_class: Class G Felony
elements: Defendant endangered the safety of another person
By recklessly operating or handling a firearm or dangerous weapon
notes: Includes reckless discharge of a firearm. Operating a firearm while intoxicated is a separate Class H Felony under § 941.20(1)(b).

statute_title: Unauthorized Use of Personal Identifying Information (Identity Theft)
offense_class: Class H Felony
elements: Defendant intentionally used or attempted to use personal identifying information of another
To obtain credit, money, goods, services, or anything of value
Without the authorization or consent of the individual
enhancements: Victim is an elder (enhanced sentencing consideration)
notes: Includes use of Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, financial account numbers. Restitution to victims required.

offense_class: Same value tiers as general theft: Class A Misdemeanor through Class F Felony
penalty_max: Same as general theft by value
fine_max: Same as general theft by value
elements: Defendant was entrusted with property of another by virtue of a fiduciary relationship
Defendant intentionally used, transferred, or concealed the property
Without the owner's consent and with intent to convert
notes: Wisconsin does not have a separate embezzlement statute. Embezzlement is prosecuted as theft by bailee under the general theft statute.

offense_class: Class H Felony
elements: Defendant falsely made or altered a writing
With intent to defraud
Writing purports to have been made by another person
notes: Uttering a forged instrument is also a Class H Felony under the same statute. Includes checks, deeds, contracts, and public documents.

offense_class: Same value tiers as general theft
penalty_max: Same as general theft by value
fine_max: Same as general theft by value
elements: Defendant obtained property or services from another
By intentionally deceiving through false representation
With intent to defraud
notes: Fraud is prosecuted under the theft statute as theft by false representation. Insurance fraud has specific statutes under § 943.395.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (under $2,500); Class I Felony ($2,500+)
elements: Defendant used a financial transaction card (credit/debit card)
Knowing it was stolen, forged, or revoked
To obtain money, goods, or services
notes: Includes possession of a stolen or forged card, card number theft, and unauthorized use. Multiple transactions may be aggregated.

offense_class: Class E Felony
elements: Defendant received or acquired proceeds known to be derived from criminal activity
Or used such proceeds to acquire property
Or conducted a financial transaction designed to conceal criminal proceeds
notes: Prosecuted under Wisconsin's RICO statute. Forfeiture of proceeds and property authorized.

offense_class: Class C Felony
elements: Defendant had sexual contact or intercourse with another person
By use or threat of force or violence
Or without consent
Or while the victim was incapable of consent
enhancements: Use of dangerous weapon (first degree — Class B Felony)
Causing pregnancy, great bodily harm, or injury (first degree)
notes: Second-degree is the most commonly charged sexual assault. First-degree (§ 940.225(1)) is a Class B Felony requiring use of weapon or causing great bodily harm.

offense_class: Class B Felony
elements: Defendant had sexual contact or intercourse with another person
Without consent and by use of a dangerous weapon
Or causing great bodily harm
Or aided by one or more persons using force or threat of force
notes: Wisconsin uses 'sexual assault' rather than 'rape.' First-degree is the most serious — requires weapon, great bodily harm, or multiple assailants. Sex offender registration required.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class I Felony (second+)
elements: Defendant committed an indecent act of sexual gratification
In public or within view of the public
Or exposed genitals or pubic area in a public or semi-public place
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class I Felony)
notes: First offense is a misdemeanor. Second or subsequent is a felony. May trigger sex offender registration depending on circumstances.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class I Felony (second+); Class H Felony (if minor)
elements: Defendant entered or remained in a place of prostitution
With intent to engage in sexual activity for a fee
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense (Class I Felony)
notes: Promoting prostitution (keeping a place of prostitution, § 944.34) is a Class H Felony. Sex trafficking of a child is a Class C Felony.

offense_class: Class C Felony
elements: Defendant employed, used, or permitted a child to engage in sexually explicit conduct
For the purpose of recording or displaying it
notes: Possession of child pornography (§ 948.12) is a Class D Felony. Distribution is a Class C Felony. Registration as sex offender required.

statute_title: Failure to Comply with Sex Offender Registration
offense_class: Class H Felony
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender
Defendant knowingly failed to register, update, or verify registration
notes: Registration requirements vary by offense: 15 years, lifetime, or GPS monitoring. Failure to register is always a felony.

statute_title: Second-Degree Sexual Assault of a Child
offense_class: Class C Felony
elements: Defendant had sexual contact or intercourse with a person under 16
Defendant was 18 years of age or older
enhancements: Victim under 13 (first degree — Class B Felony, up to 60 years)
notes: Wisconsin's age of consent is 18 for position of authority, 16 general. Sexual assault of a child under 13 is first-degree (§ 948.02(1)) — Class B Felony.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant engaged in violent, abusive, indecent, profane, boisterous, unreasonably loud, or otherwise disorderly conduct
Under circumstances in which such conduct tends to cause or provoke a disturbance
enhancements: Domestic abuse modifier (if involving household member)
notes: Disorderly conduct is the most commonly charged misdemeanor in Wisconsin. Often used as a plea-down from more serious charges including DV.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (basic); Class I Felony (if causing injury); Class H Felony (if causing substantial bodily harm)
elements: A peace officer was acting in an official capacity
Defendant knowingly resisted or obstructed the officer
enhancements: Causing injury to officer (Class I Felony)
Causing substantial bodily harm (Class H Felony)
notes: Does not require physical force — verbal obstruction, giving false information, or fleeing on foot sufficient. Separate from fleeing in a vehicle (§ 346.04).

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (obstructing officer); Class I Felony (obstructing justice — destroying evidence)
elements: Defendant knowingly gave false information to an officer
Or concealed or destroyed evidence
With intent to hinder an investigation or prosecution
notes: Obstructing an officer is commonly charged alongside resisting arrest. Destroying evidence is a separate felony.

offense_class: Criminal contempt (punitive); Civil contempt (remedial)
penalty_max: 7 days or $2,000 fine per occurrence (summary); greater for non-summary
elements: Defendant willfully disobeyed a court order
Or engaged in disorderly or disrespectful conduct in court
notes: Summary contempt may be imposed immediately for in-court misconduct. Non-summary contempt requires notice and hearing. Remedial contempt uses coercive sanctions.

offense_class: Civil forfeiture (not criminal)
elements: Defendant was intoxicated in a public place
Specifically on premises licensed for alcohol sale
notes: Wisconsin does not have a general public intoxication crime. Being drunk in public is not itself illegal. Intoxicated persons on licensed premises may be a civil forfeiture. Disorderly conduct may be charged if behavior is disruptive.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (if underlying is misdemeanor); Class H Felony (if underlying is felony)
elements: Defendant was released from custody by court order
With a condition of bail (including appearing at future hearings)
Defendant intentionally failed to comply with the terms of release
notes: Wisconsin bail jumping is unique — it criminalizes ANY violation of a bail condition, not just failure to appear. If the underlying charge is a felony, bail jumping is a Class H Felony.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant knowingly gave false information to an officer
With intent to mislead the officer in the performance of official duties
notes: Filing a false police report is charged under the obstruction statute. Bomb threats and false emergency reports have specific enhanced statutes.

statute_title: Threat to a Law Enforcement Officer, Judge, Prosecutor, or Other Person
offense_class: Class I Felony (threat to official); Class A Misdemeanor (general threat)
elements: Defendant made a threat to cause bodily harm or death to another person
With intent to frighten or intimidate
enhancements: Threat to judge, prosecutor, or law enforcement officer (Class I Felony)
notes: General threats may be charged as disorderly conduct. Threats against certain officials are specifically enhanced to felony.

offense_class: Class H Felony
elements: Defendant made a false material statement
Under oath in an official proceeding or on a document required by law
Knowing the statement was false
notes: False swearing in non-official matters is a Class A Misdemeanor. Subornation of perjury carries the same penalty.

statute_title: Bribery of Public Officers and Employees
offense_class: Class H Felony
elements: Defendant offered, gave, or agreed to give a benefit
To a public officer or employee
With intent to influence the officer's official actions
notes: Accepting a bribe (§ 946.12) is also a Class H Felony. Commercial bribery (§ 134.05) is a separate offense.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (misdemeanor custody); Class H Felony (felony custody)
elements: Defendant was lawfully in custody or confinement
Defendant intentionally escaped from custody or confinement
enhancements: Use of force or violence during escape
notes: Escape severity depends on the custody level. Failure to report to jail is also charged under this statute.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (basic); Class I Felony (intentional/repeated); Class H Felony (death or torture)
elements: Defendant treated an animal in a cruel manner
Or caused unnecessary suffering or injury to an animal
enhancements: Causing death or disfigurement (Class H Felony)
notes: Animal fighting is a separate Class I Felony. Felony animal cruelty may result in prohibition from owning animals.

offense_class: Varies — court may revoke probation and impose original sentence
elements: Defendant was placed on probation
Defendant violated a condition of probation
notes: Department of Corrections may hold revocation hearing. Alternatives to revocation include sanctions, treatment programs, and modified conditions.

offense_class: Varies — return to prison for remaining term
penalty_max: Remaining extended supervision time reconverted to imprisonment
elements: Defendant was on extended supervision or parole
Defendant violated a condition of supervision
notes: Wisconsin largely replaced traditional parole with 'extended supervision.' Revocation sends the person to prison for the remaining extended supervision time.

statute_title: Parties to Crime — Aiding and Abetting
offense_class: Same as principal offense
elements: Defendant directly committed the crime, or aided and abetted its commission
Defendant was a party to a conspiracy to commit the crime
Or defendant advised, hired, counseled, or conspired with another to commit the crime
notes: All parties to a crime are equally liable in Wisconsin. Mere presence is not sufficient — must show intentional assistance.

offense_class: Same as the completed offense
elements: Defendant had intent to commit a specific crime
Defendant performed acts indicating unequivocal intent to commit the crime
Defendant would have committed the crime except for intervention or failure of means
notes: Wisconsin punishes attempts at the same level as the completed offense — no mandatory reduction. Voluntary abandonment is an affirmative defense.

offense_class: Same felony class as the target offense (if felony); Class A Misdemeanor (if target is misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to commit a felony
An act was performed in furtherance of the conspiracy
notes: Conspiracy to commit a felony is punished at the same level as the target felony. Conspiracy to commit a misdemeanor is a Class A Misdemeanor.
